item.title: Hirome Market: Kochi's Lively Food Hall — Guide
item.description: Hirome Market is the beating heart of Kochi’s food culture, a lively covered hall in the city centre packed with dozens of small stalls and communal tables where locals eat, drink and socialise from morning till late. The undisputed star is katsuo no tataki — bonito seared over a fierce straw fire until smoky outside and rare within, sliced thick and served with garlic, salt or citrus ponzu. Around it you’ll find sashimi, fried treats, dumplings, local sake and much more, bought from whichever stall tempts you and eaten together at shared tables in a warm, boisterous atmosphere.

item.title: Katsuo Tataki Cooking Class in Kochi — Guide
item.description: One of the most memorable food experiences in Kochi is searing your own katsuo tataki over a blazing straw fire. Hands-on classes and ‘warayaki’ (straw-grilling) experiences let visitors skewer a side of bonito and hold it over towering flames of burning rice straw, watching the surface char and smoke in dramatic fashion before it is sliced and dressed. It’s part cooking lesson, part spectacle — the flames leap impressively high — and the reward is eating tataki you seared yourself, fresher and more satisfying for the effort.

item.title: Katsuo Tataki: Kochi's Seared Bonito — Guide
item.description: Katsuo no tataki is the definitive dish of Kochi, historically the province of Tosa, and one of Japan’s great regional specialities. A whole side of bonito is skewered and seared over a fierce blaze of burning rice straw, which chars and smokes the surface in seconds while leaving the inside raw and ruby-red. Sliced thick, it is served most famously ‘shio-tataki’ with just salt and garlic, or with tangy citrus ponzu, raw garlic, ginger and myoga.

item.title: Kochi Food Guide: Katsuo Tataki, Hirome Market, and Tosa Cuisine
item.description: Kochi’s food culture is confident and characterful in a way that reflects the prefecture’s historical independence. The Tosa domain was famously resistant to central authority during the Edo period, and something of that spirit persists in the local approach to eating: bold flavours, generous portions, a preference for raw or minimally processed ingredients, and a strong attachment to local production. The defining dish — katsuo tataki, seared bonito — is one of the most distinctive preparations in Japanese cuisine, and eating it in Kochi using the local wood-fire technique and the season’s first or last bonito is a genuinely different experience from encountering it elsewhere.
